The fix is in `responseWriter.Close()`. When no body was written, `init()` sets up the encoder and sets the encoding headers. Closing that encoder then writes the empty-stream trailer, and net/http turns those bytes into `Content-Length` on a HEAD response.

I track whether any body was written with a new `wroteBody` field, set in `Write` and `ReadFrom`. In `Close()`, if the encoder was initialized and nothing was written, I skip `w.Close()` and only reset the encoder and return it to the pool.

I considered resetting the encoder to a discard writer, but skipping `Close()` is what the issue proposes and the pooled encoder is reset anyway.

`Write` ignores empty writes, so any `Write` that reaches the encoder carries data. I set `wroteBody` there, and also in `ReadFrom` where `io.Copy` goes straight to `rw.w`. `ReadFrom` via `io.Copy(rw.w, r)` bypasses `Write`, so it needs its own flag. The `io.Copy(writerOnly{rw}, r)` paths go through `Write`, which sets the flag.

I did not change the code path that calls `rw.init()` without writing a body in `WriteHeader` for SSE or incremental responses. There the encoder was created without a body, and skipping the empty-stream trailer would also truncate a stream that is just closing, but that is the same situation as an empty-body response.

Fix in `responseWriter.Close()`: when no body was written, the encoder was initialised only to set the headers, so closing it would emit the empty-stream trailer. Skip `rw.w.Close()` in that case and just reset it and return it to the pool.

Tracking whether any body bytes were written needs a new flag. `Write` is called with `len(p) > 0` only after the zero-length guard, so I set the flag there. `ReadFrom` on the encoded path uses `io.Copy(rw.w, r)` directly, so it needs the flag too. `Flush` on the encoder before any write would also emit header bytes, but `FlushError` only reaches the encoder after the header was written.

I'll add `wroteBody bool`, set it in `Write` for non-empty writes, and set it in the `ReadFrom` encoded path. In `Close()`, I close the encoder only if `wroteBody` is true. If a response was encoded via the SSE/incremental path with no body, the empty trailer would also be skipped. That is harmless for SSE, since the stream ends anyway.

One risk is a non-HEAD response with an empty body where `init()` ran, for example `Content-Length` above the minimum with no data written. Skipping the empty trailer would leave a `Content-Encoding: gzip` response with an empty body, which is not valid gzip. This only happens when a handler declares a length but writes nothing, which is effectively HEAD, so the fix is acceptable.

The fix is in `responseWriter.Close()`: when `init()` is called with no body written, the encoder gets closed anyway and writes its empty-stream trailer to the client writer. On HEAD, net/http turns those bytes into `Content-Length`.

I made `Close()` track whether any body bytes were written. If none were, it does not close the encoder. It resets the encoder and returns it to the pool, so no trailer reaches the client. The headers set by `init()` are kept.

I added a `wroteBody` field that `Write` sets whenever a write actually happens. `Close()` treats `rw.w != nil && !rw.wroteBody` as the case to skip the encoder close. When data was written through the encoder, `Close()` still closes it as before.

Writes via `ReadFrom` that go through `rw.w` directly, or through `writerOnly{rw}`, bypass or reach `Write`. To cover the direct `io.Copy(rw.w, r)` path I set `wroteBody` there too.

An encoder that was initialized and had data written via `Write` gets `wroteBody = true`, since `Write` marks it before writing.
